4700:
When "divine" is used as a noun, it refers to a person of the clergy or a theologian — someone who has dedicated their life to the study, teaching, or practice of religious faith. In plain terms: a priest, a minister, a pastor, or a religious scholar who is deeply learned in theology (the study of God and religious belief).

Think of it this way: just as a native can mean a person who belongs to a place, a divine means a person who belongs to — or serves — the domain of God and religion.

"The divines of the church gathered to settle the dispute over scripture."

Here, "divines" simply means a group of learned clergy or theologians.

This is a formal and somewhat old-fashioned word. You won't hear it in everyday conversation today, but you will encounter it frequently in historical texts, literature, philosophy, and religious writings — especially from the 16th to 19th centuries. For example, the famous "Westminster Assembly of Divines" (1643) was a gathering of theologians convened to reform the English church.

There is a second, distinct usage of "divine" as a noun — when it appears as "the Divine" (usually capitalized, always with the). Here, it does not refer to a person. Instead, it refers to God, or the quality of being God, or the sacred spiritual power that underlies all existence.

This usage is abstract and philosophical. It captures the idea of the supreme, the holy, the infinite — whatever a person or tradition considers to be the ultimate spiritual reality.

"Artists have long tried to capture the Divine in their work."
"She felt a deep yearning to connect with the Divine."
"Many philosophers have argued about the nature of the Divine."

Notice that in this usage, "the Divine" stands in for something vast and sacred — it is a way of talking about God or ultimate holiness without naming any specific religion or deity. It is often preferred in philosophical, mystical, or interfaith contexts precisely because it is broad and non-sectarian.
Two Distinct Usages, Side by Side

To keep it clear in your mind:

  • "A divine" / "the divines" → a person (a clergyman or theologian). Countable. Old-fashioned.
  • "The Divine" → an abstract idea (God, the sacred, the holy). Uncountable. Still in active use in philosophy, spirituality, and literature.

"A divine" (meaning a clergy member or theologian) appears almost exclusively in:

  • Historical writing and documents
  • Classic English literature (Shakespeare's era through the Victorian era)
  • Academic writing about religion and history

You would not call a modern priest "a divine" in casual speech — it would sound archaic. But if you're reading older texts or writing in a formal, literary style, it fits perfectly.

"The Divine" (meaning God or the sacred) is alive and well today. You'll find it in:

  • Philosophy of religion
  • Mystical and spiritual writing (across many traditions — Christian, Hindu, Sufi, New Age, etc.)
  • Poetry and literary prose
  • Interfaith dialogue, where a neutral term for the sacred is useful

Both uses of "divine" as a noun share the same root idea: something — or someone — connected to God or to the highest spiritual reality. Whether it is a theologian who spends his life studying God ("a divine"), or the infinite sacred presence itself ("the Divine"), the word always carries a sense of the holy, the elevated, and the transcendent.

If you ever see "divine" in a text and you're unsure which meaning applies, ask yourself: Is it referring to a person, or to an abstract spiritual idea? That distinction will always guide you to the right meaning.
4701:
To divine something means to discover or figure out something hidden, unknown, or unclear — not by being told directly, and not through obvious logic, but through a special kind of sensing, intuition, or supernatural power.

Think of it this way: when you know something without anyone explaining it to you, and without a clear, step-by-step reason for knowing it — as if the answer came to you from some invisible source — that is the spirit of divining.

This verb operates on two levels that sit right next to each other. Understanding both will give you the complete picture.

1. The Everyday, Human Level — Intuitive Discovery

In ordinary, modern usage, to divine something means to perceive or figure out something that is not obvious, using sharp intuition or instinct.

It is similar to "sensing" or "guessing," but it is stronger and more accurate than a random guess. The person who divines something arrives at a correct understanding through a kind of deep, almost mysterious inner perception — not through someone handing them the answer.

Examples:

  • "Somehow, she divined exactly what he was feeling, even though he said nothing."
  • "The detective divined the killer's next move before any evidence pointed that way."
  • "He couldn't explain how, but he divined that something was wrong the moment he walked into the room."

Notice that in all these cases, the person knows something they were never explicitly told. There's a gap between the available information and the conclusion — and divining is what bridges that gap.

2. The Supernatural, Ancient Level — Magical or Mystical Discovery

At its deeper, more traditional level, to divine means to use supernatural or mystical means to uncover hidden truths, find hidden things, or predict what will happen in the future.

This is where the word carries a sense of magic, prophecy, and the sacred. Historically, certain people — called diviners — were believed to have special powers to read signs invisible to ordinary people: the flight of birds, the patterns in fire, the stars, or the lines of a palm.

Examples:

  • "The ancient priest claimed to divine the will of the gods from the way the smoke rose."
  • "She divined the future by reading the pattern of tea leaves in the cup."
  • "The shaman was called to divine the location of the missing child."

One very specific and well-known use is water divining (also called dowsing) — the practice of walking across land holding a forked stick, which is believed to bend and point downward when underground water is below. The person doing this is called a water diviner. Whether or not this actually works is debated, but the practice itself is very real and historically widespread.
The Key Quality That Unites Both Meanings

Whether it is intuitive or supernatural, the act of divining always involves:

  • Something that is hidden, unclear, or not directly available
  • A person who reaches through that invisibility to find the truth
  • A method that goes beyond ordinary reasoning or physical evidence

This is what separates divining from simply figuring something out. When you figure something out, you can usually explain the steps you took. When you divine something, the process feels almost inexplicable — as if the knowledge came from somewhere beyond the normal, visible world.
The Related Words You Will Encounter

Understanding the verb is incomplete without knowing its close family:

  • Diviner — a person who divines; someone with the gift or practice of finding hidden truths. "The village diviner was consulted whenever livestock went missing."
  • Divination — the noun for the broader practice or art of divining, especially through supernatural methods. "Ancient civilizations relied heavily on divination before going to war." Divination includes things like reading tarot cards, consulting oracles, astrology, and reading omens.
  • Divined — past tense. "She divined his intentions before he even opened his mouth."
  • Divining — present participle, used for ongoing action. "He spent his life divining the secrets of the universe."
How It Feels — The Tone of the Word

This verb carries a quietly powerful and slightly mysterious tone. It is not a casual word. When a writer uses divine as a verb, they are suggesting that the knowledge gained is special — almost gifted, almost otherworldly. It elevates the act of discovery into something more than ordinary.

If someone says "he guessed what I was thinking," it sounds lucky or coincidental. But if someone says "he divined what I was thinking," it sounds like he reached into something deep and unseen and pulled out the truth — which is a much more striking and impressive image.

To divine is to discover something hidden or unknown — either through a deep, almost supernatural intuition (in everyday use), or through an actual mystical or magical practice (in its traditional sense) — in a way that goes beyond ordinary seeing or reasoning.
4702:
When something is divisive, it causes people to split into opposing sides. It creates sharp disagreement, tension, or conflict — pulling people apart rather than bringing them together.

Think of it like a knife cutting a group of people in half. On one side are those who strongly support something; on the other side are those who strongly oppose it. The thing that caused that split is divisive.

Almost anything can be divisive — a topic, a person, a decision, a policy, a statement, a piece of art, or even a choice made at work. What matters is not what it is, but what it does: it causes people to disagree strongly and take opposing sides.

Politics: A new tax law that some people love and others deeply hate is divisive. It doesn't just create mild disagreement — it creates passionate, opposing camps.

Society: Topics like immigration, gun control, or capital punishment are often called divisive because they reliably split entire populations into strongly opposed groups.

Workplace: A manager who openly favors certain employees over others can be divisive — their behavior creates tension, jealousy, and conflict within the team.

Sports: Imagine a referee makes a questionable call in a big game. Half the fans think it was fair; the other half think it was outrageous. That call was divisive.

Art & Culture: A controversial film, book, or song that causes half the audience to praise it and the other half to condemn it is divisive.
The Key Ingredient: Strong, Opposing Reactions

For something to be truly divisive, the disagreement it creates must be strong. If people have mildly different opinions, we wouldn't usually call it divisive. The word implies a deep, passionate split — often one where both sides feel very strongly and find it hard to meet in the middle.

It also implies that the disagreement is more than just intellectual — it often carries emotion. People don't just think differently; they may feel frustrated, angry, or upset with those on the other side.

Divisive almost always carries a negative or critical tone. When you call something divisive, you are usually suggesting it is harmful or undesirable — that it is tearing a community, country, group, or relationship apart.

For example:

  • "The president's speech was divisive." — This implies the speech caused unnecessary conflict and split people apart, and the speaker probably disapproves of this outcome.
  • "We need to move away from divisive rhetoric." — This means: we need to stop using language that inflames conflict and turns people against each other.

However, the word itself does not make a moral judgment about who is right. It simply describes the effect — that something causes division. Both sides of a divisive debate can be right or wrong; the word only tells you that the split exists and is sharp.

• It does not mean simply "controversial." A controversial thing sparks debate and discussion, but a divisive thing specifically splits people into opposing camps with strong feeling. All divisive things tend to be controversial, but not all controversial things are divisive.
  • It does not mean "difficult" or "complicated." A math problem can be difficult, but not divisive. Divisive is specifically about people being pulled apart.
  • It does not require a 50/50 split. Even if 80% of people support something, if the remaining 20% oppose it passionately and the disagreement creates real tension and conflict, it can still be called divisive.
Who or What Gets Called Divisive

The word is used to describe:

  • Issues/topics — "Abortion is one of the most divisive issues in modern politics."
  • People — "He is a divisive figure — people either admire him greatly or despise him."
  • Actions/decisions — "The company's decision to cut salaries was divisive and damaged team morale."
  • Language/rhetoric — "The politician was criticized for using divisive language that turned communities against each other."
  • Policies — "The new school policy was divisive among parents."

To deepen your understanding, here are words that are close in meaning:

  • Polarizing — very similar; means something pushes people to extreme, opposing positions. (A polarizing figure is one people either love or hate.)
  • Contentious — causing argument and disagreement. Slightly milder than divisive.
  • Inflammatory — something that deliberately stirs up strong emotion and conflict.
  • Controversial — sparking debate and disagreement; broader and milder than divisive.

The opposite of divisive would be words like: unifying, cohesive, inclusive, harmonious — things that bring people together rather than split them apart.
Divisive describes something that causes people to split into strongly opposing sides, creating conflict, tension, and disagreement — and it almost always implies this split is unwanted or harmful.
4703:
Divisiveness is the quality of causing people to split into opposing groups that disagree with, resent, or conflict with each other. When something has divisiveness, it doesn't just create mild disagreement — it drives people apart, breaks unity, and creates tension or hostility between sides.

Think of it this way: imagine a rope being pulled from both ends until it tears in the middle. Divisiveness is the force doing the pulling.

The word comes from the idea of dividing — but not in the harmless math sense. In human terms, to divide people means to push them into separate, opposing camps where they stop seeing themselves as part of the same team.

Divisiveness is the degree to which something has that power — the power to cause that kind of split.

So when someone says, "There is a lot of divisiveness in the country right now," they mean: people in that country are deeply split — they hold strongly opposing views, they feel hostile toward those who disagree with them, and the sense of shared community is weakened or broken.
What Divisiveness Looks Like in Real Life

Divisiveness can appear in many places:

In politics: A politician who constantly portrays one group of citizens as the enemy of another is practicing divisiveness. Their words don't just express an opinion — they actively push people into hostile opposing camps.

In a workplace: A manager who plays employees against each other, shares gossip, or gives preferential treatment in ways that cause resentment is creating divisiveness in the team. People stop cooperating and start competing or distrusting each other.

In a family: A topic like inheritance, religion, or an old grudge can cause divisiveness at a family gathering — turning what should be a warm reunion into a battlefield of tension and sides.

In society: Issues like race, immigration, or religion often carry enormous divisiveness — they are topics that quickly split communities into strongly opposed groups with deep emotional investment on each side.

Divisiveness doesn't appear from nowhere. Common causes include:

  • Extreme or inflammatory language — words designed to provoke outrage and paint the "other side" as evil or dangerous.
  • Unfair treatment — when one group feels it is being treated worse than another, resentment and division grow.
  • Propaganda and misinformation — when people are fed distorted or false information, they develop very different pictures of reality, making it nearly impossible to find common ground.
  • Self-interest — sometimes leaders or groups deliberately stoke divisiveness because it benefits them (e.g., "if people are fighting each other, they won't unite against me").
  • Deep value differences — sometimes divisiveness arises genuinely because people hold fundamentally different beliefs about what is right, fair, or important.

Divisiveness is rarely the end of the story. It tends to produce consequences:

  • Erosion of trust — people stop believing those on the "other side" have good intentions.
  • Breakdown of cooperation — groups that are divided struggle to work together on shared problems.
  • Escalation — divisiveness can grow. What starts as disagreement can become hostility, and hostility can become conflict.
  • Echo chambers — divided people stop talking to each other and only interact with those who already agree with them, making the divide even deeper over time.
An Important Nuance: Not All Disagreement Is Divisiveness

This is a subtle but important distinction that many learners miss.

Disagreement is normal and healthy. People debating ideas, arguing different policies, or expressing opposing views is not, by itself, divisiveness.

Divisiveness is specifically about the tearing apart of a group's unity — usually through hostility, resentment, or the deliberate creation of an "us vs. them" mentality. The key ingredient is not just difference of opinion, but the emotional and social rupture that follows.

So: two scientists debating competing theories passionately = disagreement, not divisiveness.
But: a political leader saying "people who disagree with me are traitors and enemies" = divisiveness.

The difference is whether the conflict breaks relationships, community, and mutual respect, or simply represents a normal exchange of differing views.

Divisiveness is not always all-or-nothing. You can describe its intensity:

  • "A small amount of divisiveness" — some mild splitting, some tension.
  • "Deep divisiveness" — severe splits, strong hostility, a community or nation significantly fractured.
  • "Deliberate divisiveness" — someone is intentionally trying to create division for their own benefit.

Since you're learning, it helps to see the whole family of this word:

FormExample
Divide (verb)Conflict tends to divide communities.
Division (noun)There is a deep division between the two groups.
Divisive (adjective)His speech was deliberately divisive.
Divisiveness (noun — the one you're learning)The divisiveness of the debate shocked everyone.
Divisively (adverb)He spoke divisively, inflaming tensions.

These show the word used naturally, so you can feel how it fits:

  1. The divisiveness of the election tore friendships apart.
  2. The CEO's behavior introduced divisiveness into a team that once worked seamlessly together.
  3. Critics accused the media of spreading divisiveness by sensationalizing every conflict.
  4. Social media algorithms are often blamed for increasing political divisiveness.
  5. The community leader urged people to resist divisiveness and focus on shared goals.
  6. Years of economic inequality had bred a divisiveness that no single speech could heal.
Divisiveness is the quality of splitting people into hostile, opposing groups — breaking down unity, trust, and cooperation — whether through words, actions, policies, or ideas.
4704:
A divot is a small chunk of earth — grass, soil, and roots all stuck together — that gets scooped or torn out of the ground, leaving a little hollow behind. Think of it as a bite taken out of the ground.

The word actually carries two related meanings at once, and this is important:

  • The piece of turf that was removed → that's a divot.
  • The hole or depression left behind after the piece is gone → that's also called a divot.

Both meanings are correct and widely used. Context usually makes clear which one is meant.
Where You'll Hear It Most: Golf

The word is most at home on a golf course, and understanding golf makes the word click instantly.

When a golfer swings a club to hit the ball, the club's sharp edge sometimes digs into the turf and slices out a small, flat flap of grass and dirt. That flap — and the dent it leaves in the ground — is a divot.

Good golf etiquette requires players to "replace their divot," meaning they pick up that torn-out piece and press it back into the hole so the course stays smooth for others. You'll often see golfers carrying a small tool called a "divot repair tool" for this exact purpose.

So on a golf course:

  • "He took a big divot with that iron shot." → His club dug out a noticeable chunk of turf.
  • "The ball rolled right into a divot." → The ball landed in one of those little hollows in the ground.
  • "Please replace your divots." → A polite reminder on course signs.

The word has traveled well beyond golf. In everyday language, a divot refers to any small dent, hollow, or indentation in a surface — not just grass. The logic is the same: something is missing from a surface, leaving a little depression.

Examples:

  • "There's a divot in the drywall where the doorknob hit it." → A small dent in the wall.
  • "The car has a divot on the hood from the hailstorm." → A small rounded dent.
  • "The mattress has a divot in the middle from years of use." → A sunken, worn-down area.
  • "She had a small divot on her chin — a little natural indentation." → A slight hollow in skin.

In all these cases, the image is consistent: a small, localized depression where the surface dips inward or where material is missing.
The Key Qualities of a Divot

To use the word accurately, keep these features in mind:

  • Small in size. A divot is never a large crater or a wide ditch. It's modest — a few inches at most. If the hole is large, people reach for different words (pit, crater, trench, pothole).
  • Relatively shallow. A divot is a surface-level scoop, not a deep hole.
  • Caused by force or pressure. Divots don't form on their own — something digs, hits, or presses into the surface to create one.
  • Localized. A divot is a specific spot, not a general unevenness.

If you had to carry just one image in your head for "divot," let it be this: a golf club swinging down, slicing a little flap of turf out of the green, and leaving a shallow scooped-out hollow in the ground. That image — the missing piece and the depression it leaves — is the heart of the word. Everything else is just that same idea applied to walls, car hoods, mattresses, skin, or any other surface where a small chunk is missing or pushed in.
4705:
To divulge something means to reveal or share information that was previously private, secret, or confidential.

When you divulge something, you are taking information that was being kept hidden — either by you or someone else — and bringing it out into the open by telling someone about it.

Think of it this way: if information is locked inside a vault, divulging it means you opened the vault and let someone see what's inside.

The most important thing to understand about this word is that it almost always involves sensitive or confidential information. You wouldn't use "divulge" to talk about sharing your favourite colour or your lunch plans. The word carries a built-in sense that the information being shared is:

  • Private (meant for a limited number of people), or
  • Secret (actively kept hidden), or
  • Sensitive (something that matters whether it gets out or not)

This is what separates "divulge" from a casual word like "tell." When someone divulges something, there is a feeling of weight and significance to the act of sharing.
The Connotation: Is It Positive or Negative?

"Divulge" sits in an interesting middle ground. It can be used both neutrally and negatively, depending on the context.

Neutral use — simply meaning someone chose to share private information, with no judgment:

The doctor did not divulge the patient's medical records to anyone.
She finally divulged the recipe she had kept secret for years.

Negative use — suggesting the information was shared when it perhaps shouldn't have been, implying a breach of trust or confidentiality:

The spy was caught after divulging classified information to the enemy.
He divulged his colleague's personal struggles at the meeting, which was inappropriate.

So the word doesn't always imply wrongdoing, but it always implies that the information being shared was not freely or openly available to begin with.

"Divulge" is a transitive verb, which means it must have an object — something being divulged. You cannot just say "he divulged" and leave it there. You must say what was divulged.

Correct:

She refused to divulge the name of her source.
He divulged the details of the plan.

Incorrect:

She refused to divulge. (incomplete — divulge what?)

You can also say who the information is being divulged to:

He divulged the secret to his closest friend.
She was pressured into divulging the information to the committee.
Common Words and Phrases It Pairs With

These are the kinds of words you will most often see alongside "divulge" in real usage:

What gets divulged (the objects):

  • divulge a secret
  • divulge information / details
  • divulge a name / identity
  • divulge classified material
  • divulge confidential data
  • divulge the contents of something

Common verbal patterns:

  • refuse to divulge — (the most common pairing, meaning someone chose NOT to reveal something)
  • unwilling to divulge
  • forced to divulge
  • decline to divulge
  • asked to divulge
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Divulge" is a formal to semi-formal word. You are more likely to find it in:

  • Newspapers and journalism
  • Legal or official contexts
  • Literature and serious writing
  • Formal speech

In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to just say "tell," "share," or "let out." If someone says "I can't divulge that" in conversation, it sounds deliberate and serious — almost as if they are consciously acknowledging that the information is sensitive and protected.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Many words are close to "divulge" in meaning, but each one has its own flavour:

Tell — the most general and casual word. No implication that the information is sensitive.

She told me about her holiday.

Reveal — means to uncover or show something that was hidden. Can apply to physical things too, not just information. Less emphasis on secrecy.

He pulled back the curtain to reveal the painting.

Disclose — very formal, often used in legal, financial, or official settings. Neutral in tone, no sense of betrayal.

Companies are legally required to disclose their earnings.

Expose — implies bringing something hidden into the open, often by force, and often involves wrongdoing or scandal.

The journalist exposed the government's corruption.

Leak — implies unofficial, unauthorised, and often covert disclosure of information, usually to the media.

Someone leaked the confidential report to the press.

Divulge — sits between "disclose" and "expose." It is more personal and deliberate than "disclose," but less dramatic and scandalous than "expose." It clearly focuses on sharing what was private or secret, and it always implies the information had some level of protection or sensitivity around it.

Here are several sentences showing "divulge" used across different situations, so you can see how it works in practice:

  1. The lawyer refused to divulge what her client had told her in private.
  2. After years of silence, he finally divulged the truth about what had happened that night.
  3. The company would not divulge the terms of the deal.
  4. She was careful never to divulge her source's identity.
  5. Under questioning, the suspect divulged the location of the stolen goods.
  6. I'm not at liberty to divulge that information. (A very common phrase, meaning "I am not allowed to share that.")
  7. The chef finally agreed to divulge his secret ingredient.

If you want to remember this word in the simplest possible way:

To divulge something is to share private or secret information with someone — information that was, until that moment, being kept hidden or protected.
4706:
"Divvy up" means to divide something into portions and share those portions among a group of people.

When you divvy up something, you are essentially doing two things at once:

  1. Splitting something into parts.
  2. Distributing those parts to the people involved.

Think of it like cutting a pizza into slices and handing each slice to someone at the table. That whole action — cutting and sharing — is "divvying up."
A Simple Example to Lock It In

Imagine you and three friends collect $100 selling old books at a garage sale. You all agree to share the money equally. So each person gets $25. The act of splitting and sharing that $100 among yourselves? That is divvying it up.

"Let's divvy up the money we made."

Simple. Clean. That's the core idea.

"Divvy" is an informal, shortened form of the word "divide." It has been used in American English since at least the mid-1800s, originally as slang. Over time, it became widely accepted in everyday informal speech across English-speaking countries.

The word "up" attached to it is what linguists call a particle — a small word that adds a sense of completeness. It signals that the dividing and sharing is being done thoroughly, from start to finish. This is the same "up" you see in phrases like "clean up," "finish up," or "use up."

So "divvy up" = divide + share + completely.
The Grammar: How to Use It

"Divvy up" is a phrasal verb — that means it is a verb made of two or more words that together create a specific meaning.

Basic structure:

Subject + divvy up + the thing being divided + (among/between + the people)

Examples:

  • "We need to divvy up the chores."
  • "They divvied up the prize money among the winners."
  • "Can you divvy up these snacks between the kids?"

Notice that the past tense is "divvied up" — the "y" changes to "ied," just like "carry → carried."

You can also split the phrasal verb by placing the object in the middle:

  • "Let's divvy the bill up." ✅
  • "Let's divvy up the bill." ✅

Both are correct. However, if you use a pronoun (like it, them, this), you must place it in the middle:

  • "Let's divvy it up." ✅
  • "Let's divvy up it." ❌
Does "Divvy Up" Always Mean Equal Shares?

No. This is an important nuance.

"Divvy up" simply means to divide and distribute. It does not automatically promise that every person gets the same amount. The shares could be equal or unequal, depending on what is agreed upon.

  • Equal: "We divvied up the inheritance equally among the three siblings." (each gets the same)
  • Unequal: "They divvied up the work based on each person's skills." (each gets what suits them)

The word itself is neutral about fairness. Context tells you whether the division is equal or not.
Register: When to Use It and When Not To

"Divvy up" is an informal, conversational expression. You would use it comfortably with:

  • Friends and family
  • Casual workplace conversations
  • Everyday writing like texts or informal emails

You would avoid it in:

  • Formal writing (reports, academic papers, legal documents)
  • Professional emails to clients or senior management
  • Formal speeches

In formal contexts, replace it with: divide, distribute, allocate, apportion, or share out.

InformalFormal Equivalent

In informal speech: "Let's divvy up the tasks."
In formal writing: "The tasks will be allocated among team members."

This idiom is highly versatile. People use it with many different types of things:

Money and finances:
"The business partners divvied up the profits at the end of the year."

Food:
"She divvied up the cake so everyone at the party got a piece."

Work and responsibilities:
"Before starting the project, the team divvied up the tasks so no one was overloaded."

Physical space or territory:
"After the merger, the two companies divvied up the sales regions between them."

Time:
"The parents divvied up the school-run duties for the week."

Winnings or rewards:
"The lottery winners divvied up their prize money and went their separate ways."

As you can see, anything that can be divided and shared can be divvied up.

These phrases carry a very similar meaning and are worth knowing as a group:

  • Split up — "Let's split up the cost of the trip."
  • Share out — "She shared out the sandwiches evenly."
  • Divide up — "We divided up the leftover pizza."
  • Parcel out — "He parcelled out the duties to each volunteer."
  • Apportion (more formal) — "The budget was apportioned among the departments."

All of these involve dividing and distributing, just like "divvy up" — the key difference is that "divvy up" is the most casual and colorful of the bunch.
A Quick Summary to Remember It Forever

"Divvy up" = to take something (money, food, work, space, etc.), break it into parts, and give each part to the people who are sharing it. It is informal, friendly, and commonly used in everyday English. It does not guarantee equal shares — just that the dividing and sharing happens completely.

The next time you and a friend split the cost of something, share food, or divide tasks — you are divvying things up. It is as simple and human as that.
4707: DNA stands for Deoxyribonucleic Acid. Don't let that long name intimidate you — by the end of this guide, every word in it will make sense.
The Big Picture: What Is DNA?

Think of DNA as a master instruction manual that exists inside almost every living cell of every organism — humans, animals, plants, bacteria, and more. This manual contains all the instructions needed to build, run, and reproduce a living being.

Every single physical trait you have — your height, the color of your eyes, whether your hair is straight or curly, how your heart pumps blood, how your liver cleans toxins — all of it is ultimately determined, at least in part, by the information stored in your DNA.

DNA is also a molecule — meaning it is a physical, chemical substance, not just an abstract concept. It is made of atoms bonded together in a specific way, and it physically exists inside your cells.
Where Is DNA Found?

In humans and most other complex organisms (called eukaryotes), nearly all DNA is found inside a small, enclosed compartment in the cell called the nucleus. Think of the nucleus as a vault — it protects and houses the DNA.

However, a small additional amount of DNA is also found in the mitochondria, which are the energy-producing structures of the cell. This is called mitochondrial DNA, and it has special properties we'll touch on later.

Simpler organisms like bacteria (called prokaryotes) have no nucleus — their DNA just floats in a compact region inside the cell.
The Shape of DNA: The Double Helix

DNA has one of the most famous shapes in all of science: the double helix.

Imagine a ladder. Now imagine twisting that ladder into a long, spiral shape — like a spring or a spiral staircase. That twisted ladder is a double helix.

The two sides of the ladder (the "rails") are made of alternating units of:

  • A sugar called deoxyribose (this is where the "deoxyribo" in DNA comes from)
  • A phosphate group (a cluster of phosphorus and oxygen atoms)

The rungs of the ladder — the steps connecting the two rails — are made of pairs of chemical units called bases (also called nucleobases).
The Four Bases: The Alphabet of Life

There are exactly four bases in DNA:

  • Adenine (A)
  • Thymine (T)
  • Guanine (G)
  • Cytosine (C)

Each rung of the DNA ladder is made of two bases joined together. Here's the crucial rule: bases only pair with their specific partner:

  • A always pairs with T
  • G always pairs with C

This is called complementary base pairing, and it is one of the most important rules in all of biology. The bases are held together by weak chemical bonds called hydrogen bonds.

So when you look at the DNA ladder, each rung is either an A-T pair or a G-C pair, never any other combination.
Nucleotides: The Basic Building Block

The smallest repeating unit of DNA is called a nucleotide. Each nucleotide consists of three things bonded together:

  1. A deoxyribose sugar
  2. A phosphate group
  3. One of the four bases (A, T, G, or C)

Think of nucleotides as the individual letters in the DNA language. A whole strand of DNA is just millions of nucleotides linked together in a chain, one after another.
How Much DNA Does a Human Have?

A human cell contains approximately 3 billion base pairs of DNA. If you were to uncoil and stretch out all the DNA from a single human cell, it would be about 2 meters (6 feet) long — yet it fits inside a nucleus that is only about 6 micrometers (0.006 millimeters) wide. This is possible because DNA is coiled and packaged incredibly tightly with the help of special proteins called histones.

Across all the cells in your body (you have around 37 trillion of them), the total length of your DNA, if laid end to end, would stretch from Earth to the Sun and back about 300 times.
Chromosomes: DNA, Neatly Packaged

DNA doesn't float around loosely inside the nucleus. It is coiled tightly around histone proteins, then further coiled and compacted into structures called chromosomes.

Human cells typically contain 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs. One chromosome from each pair came from your biological mother, and the other came from your biological father.

Each chromosome contains one long, continuous DNA molecule. Chromosome 1 (the largest) contains about 249 million base pairs. Chromosome 21 (one of the smallest) contains about 47 million base pairs.
Genes: The Meaningful Segments of DNA

Not all of the DNA on a chromosome is the same. Within the long DNA sequence, there are specific segments that carry instructions for making specific molecules (mostly proteins). These functional segments are called genes.

A gene is, in simple terms, a stretch of DNA that encodes a particular protein or has a specific biological function.

The human genome contains approximately 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes. But here is a surprising fact: these genes only account for about 1–2% of the total DNA. The rest of the DNA — sometimes historically called "junk DNA" — is now known to serve various regulatory, structural, and other functions, though some of it may truly be non-functional remnants of evolution.
What Does DNA Actually Do? The Central Dogma

The most important job of DNA is to carry the instructions for making proteins. Proteins are the workhorses of biology — they build structures, carry oxygen, fight infections, speed up chemical reactions, send signals, and perform thousands of other functions.

The flow of biological information goes like this:

DNA → RNA → Protein

This is called the Central Dogma of Molecular Biology. Let's break it down:

Step 1: Transcription (DNA → RNA)

When a gene needs to be "read," the relevant segment of DNA is copied into a related molecule called messenger RNA (mRNA). RNA is similar to DNA but single-stranded and uses a slightly different sugar (ribose instead of deoxyribose) and a slightly different base — Uracil (U) instead of Thymine (T).

This copying process is called transcription and is carried out by an enzyme called RNA polymerase. Think of transcription as photocopying a page from the master instruction book (DNA) to carry the message outside the vault (nucleus).

Step 2: Translation (RNA → Protein)

The mRNA travels out of the nucleus to structures called ribosomes in the cell. There, the sequence of bases in the mRNA is read in groups of three, called codons. Each codon specifies a particular amino acid (the building blocks of proteins). A specific type of RNA called transfer RNA (tRNA) brings the right amino acid to each codon. The amino acids are linked together, one by one, forming a chain — and that chain folds into a functional protein.

The genetic code (the system by which codons map to amino acids) is nearly universal — the same codons mean the same amino acids in bacteria, plants, and humans. This is profound evidence that all life on Earth shares a common ancestor.
DNA Replication: Copying the Instruction Manual

Every time a cell divides, it needs to pass a complete copy of its DNA to each daughter cell. This is done through a process called DNA replication.

The double helix "unzips" — the two strands separate along their base pairs. Each single strand then serves as a template to build a new complementary strand. Because of the A-T and G-C base pairing rules, each new strand is an exact copy of the original.

This is carried out by a group of enzymes, the most important being DNA polymerase. The result is two identical DNA double helices where there was originally one. Each new double helix contains one original strand and one newly made strand — this is called semi-conservative replication.

The replication process is remarkably accurate — DNA polymerase makes roughly only one error per billion base pairs copied, and most errors are caught and corrected by built-in proofreading mechanisms.
Mutations: Errors in the Code

Occasionally, a mistake in the DNA sequence is not corrected. This is called a mutation. Mutations can arise from:

  • Replication errors during cell division
  • Environmental damage (UV radiation from sunlight, X-rays, certain chemicals)
  • Spontaneous chemical changes in the bases

Mutations can be as small as a single base change (called a point mutation or SNP — single nucleotide polymorphism), or as large as entire sections of chromosomes being deleted, duplicated, or rearranged.

Most mutations have no effect (they fall in non-coding regions), some are beneficial (they can drive evolution), and some are harmful (they can disrupt protein function and cause diseases like cancer or genetic disorders).
DNA and Heredity: How Traits Are Passed Down

This brings us to the reason DNA became so central to biology — inheritance.

When organisms reproduce sexually (as humans do), each parent contributes half their chromosomes to the offspring through specialized reproductive cells called gametes (sperm and egg). Each gamete contains 23 chromosomes (half the normal 46). When a sperm fertilizes an egg, the resulting cell (called a zygote) has the full 46 chromosomes — 23 from each parent.

This is why children resemble both parents but are not identical to either — they receive a unique mix of DNA from both. Except for identical twins (who arise from the same fertilized egg), every human being who has ever lived has a unique DNA sequence.
DNA and Identity: Why You Are Unique

Across the 3 billion base pairs in your genome, most of your DNA (about 99.9%) is identical to every other human being. It's that 0.1% variation — roughly 3 million base pairs — that makes you genetically distinct from every other person on Earth.

This is the basis of DNA fingerprinting (also called DNA profiling) — a forensic technique used in criminal investigations, paternity tests, and identifying disaster victims. Because your DNA profile is unique to you, it can serve as a biological "fingerprint."
Mitochondrial DNA: A Special Case

As mentioned earlier, mitochondria have their own small circular DNA molecule, separate from the DNA in the nucleus. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost exclusively from the mother (since the egg cell's mitochondria dominate after fertilization). This makes it extremely useful for tracing maternal ancestry and studying human migration patterns throughout history.
Epigenetics: Not Just the Sequence

A crucial modern insight is that biology is not controlled purely by the DNA sequence itself. Epigenetics is the study of changes in gene activity that do not involve changes to the DNA sequence. Chemical modifications to histones and the DNA itself (like adding a methyl group — called methylation) can turn genes "on" or "off" without changing the underlying code.

Epigenetic marks can be influenced by environment, diet, stress, and aging — and some can even be passed to the next generation. This means who you are isn't determined by your DNA sequence alone; it's also about which genes are active at any given time.
A Brief History of DNA

• 1869 — Friedrich Miescher first isolated DNA from white blood cells, calling it "nuclein."
  • 1944 — Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty showed that DNA (not protein) carries genetic information.
  • 1952 — Rosalind Franklin took X-ray crystallography images of DNA that were critical to discovering its structure.
  • 1953 — James Watson and Francis Crick, using Franklin's data, proposed the double helix model of DNA, published in Nature.
  • 1961 — The genetic code (codons → amino acids) was cracked by Marshall Nirenberg and colleagues.
  • 2003 — The Human Genome Project was completed, mapping the entire sequence of human DNA for the first time.
So, To Summarize

ConceptIn Plain Words

DNA is the molecule of life. It is a long, double-stranded, helical molecule made of four types of chemical "letters" (A, T, G, C). The sequence of these letters encodes instructions — primarily for making proteins — that determine how every living organism is built and how it functions. DNA is packed into chromosomes inside the cell's nucleus. Specific segments of DNA called genes are read and translated into proteins through the processes of transcription and translation. DNA copies itself faithfully when cells divide, passes genetic information from parents to children, and can undergo mutations that drive both disease and evolution. The story of DNA is, in many ways, the story of life itself.
4708:
To do a number on someone or something means to harm, damage, hurt, or have a strong negative effect on someone or something — physically, emotionally, or psychologically. It can also mean to deceive, manipulate, or trick someone in a harmful way.

Think of it this way: when someone or something "does a number on" a person or thing, the result is that the person or thing ends up worse off than before — beaten down, messed up, tricked, or deeply affected.
Breaking It Down Simply

Imagine a boxer enters a fight. His opponent punches him so hard and so repeatedly that he comes out looking terrible — bruised, broken, and defeated. You could say:

"His opponent really did a number on him."

Now take that same idea and apply it to emotions, health, confidence, finances, or any other aspect of life — the idiom works the same way. Whatever the "number" was done on, it ended up significantly worse or damaged.
The Two Main Shades of Meaning

This idiom carries two closely related but slightly different meanings, and understanding both will give you full command of it.

1. To Cause Serious Harm or Damage

This is the most common use. It means something or someone inflicted serious damage — physical, emotional, financial, or otherwise — on a person or thing.

  • The harsh winter did a number on the roads. (The roads got badly damaged.)
  • That surgery really did a number on his body. (His body suffered a lot.)
  • Losing her job did a number on her self-esteem. (Her self-esteem took a serious hit.)
  • The flood did a number on the old farmhouse. (The farmhouse was severely damaged.)

Notice that the "harm" doesn't have to be physical. It can be emotional, psychological, or even abstract — like damage to a reputation, finances, or mental health.

2. To Deceive, Manipulate, or Con Someone

This meaning is a bit more specific. Here, someone tricks, cheats, or psychologically manipulates another person, often to gain something or to control them.

  • That salesman really did a number on her — she paid twice the price she should have.
  • His ex-partner did a number on him, convincing him he was worthless.
  • The con artist did a number on the entire village.

In this sense, there's an element of intentional trickery or psychological manipulation — someone is being played or fooled, and they end up hurt or worse off because of it.
The Key Emotion Behind the Idiom

Whether the meaning leans toward harm or deception, the feeling behind this idiom is almost always one of being overpowered, overwhelmed, or left in a bad state. The subject (the person or thing that the number is "done on") is the victim — they didn't have control over what happened to them.
Origin: Where Did This Come From?

The word "number" has long been used in entertainment to refer to a performance piece — a song, dance, comedy act, or magic trick is called a "number." Think of a magician performing a trick: it is his "number," his act, his performance.

Over time, the phrase "do a number" started to be used in informal and criminal slang to mean performing a deceptive act or a "job" on someone — pulling off a scheme, trick, or piece of manipulation against a target. Like a skilled performer pulling off a spectacular (but harmful) trick.

From there, the meaning expanded beyond just deception to include any kind of strong, damaging effect — because both deception and physical damage leave the victim feeling the same way: beaten and wrecked.

The idiom became widespread in American English during the 20th century and is now used in everyday informal speech across the English-speaking world.
Grammar and Structure

The idiom follows this structure:

do + a number + on + [person or thing]

The verb "do" is conjugated based on tense and subject:

  • The stress is doing a number on my health. (present continuous)
  • The accident did a number on the car. (simple past)
  • Criticism can do a number on a person's confidence. (general truth)
  • The cold weather has done a number on the pipes. (present perfect)

You can also intensify it with words like "really," "quite," "quite a," or "one hell of a":

  • That really did a number on him.
  • The injury did quite a number on her knee.
Register: When and Where Is This Used?

This is an informal, colloquial idiom. You will hear it in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Informal writing (blogs, social media, casual emails)
  • Journalism and news articles (when writing in a conversational tone)
  • Movies, TV shows, and novels

You would not typically use it in formal academic writing or professional business documents. In those settings, you would say something like "severely damaged," "had a serious detrimental effect on," or "significantly harmed."
Real-World Example Sentences Across Contexts

Health and body:

  • Years of heavy lifting really did a number on his back.
  • That flu did a number on her — she couldn't get out of bed for a week.

Mental health and emotions:

  • The breakup did a number on his confidence.
  • Growing up in an unstable home did a number on her ability to trust people.

Finances:

  • The economic crisis did a number on their savings.
  • The unexpected legal fees did a number on the company's budget.

Physical objects:

  • The storm did a number on the roof.
  • Years of neglect really did a number on that old car.

Deception/manipulation:

  • That recruiter did a number on me — none of the job details were as described.
  • She realized her so-called friend had been doing a number on her for years, slowly isolating her from everyone she knew.
What It Does NOT Mean

To avoid confusion, here are things this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean to do something positive or helpful. It is almost always negative.
  • It does not simply mean "to do something to someone." The impact must be significantly damaging.
  • It does not refer to a literal number (like 1, 2, 3) in any way.
Similar Idioms and Expressions

These idioms carry overlapping meanings and are useful to know alongside this one:

  • "Take a toll on" — to gradually wear something or someone down. (The long hours took a toll on her health.)
  • "Wreak havoc on" — to cause great chaos or damage. (The virus wreaked havoc on the economy.)
  • "Put someone through the wringer" — to cause someone to go through a very difficult or exhausting experience.
  • "Pull a fast one on someone" — to trick or deceive someone. (More focused on deception.)
  • "Do a job on someone" — very similar in meaning; to harm or damage someone significantly.
Quick Summary

MeaningTo seriously harm, damage, hurt, or deceive someone or something
ToneAlways negative; the victim ends up worse off
RegisterInformal / colloquial
OriginFrom "number" as a performance trick; later slang for a harmful scheme or act
Used onPeople, emotions, objects, finances, health, relationships — almost anything

In short, whenever you see or hear "did/does/doing a number on," picture something being beaten up, tricked, or badly damaged. That mental image will serve you perfectly every time.
4709:
"Do in" is a phrasal verb — a main verb ("do") combined with a small particle ("in") that together produce a meaning you cannot guess just from the two words alone. This is what makes phrasal verbs tricky for learners: "do" means one thing on its own, and "in" means another, but together they create something new.

"Do in" is informal and colloquial, meaning it belongs in everyday speech, casual writing, texts, films, and novels — not in formal essays or professional emails.

It has four distinct meanings. All four share the same dark thread: bringing something to a ruinous, painful, or final end — whether that end is a person's life, your physical energy, your body, or someone's reputation.

Meaning 1 — To Kill Someone

This is the most dramatic meaning and the one most associated with crime fiction, thrillers, and gangster films.

"To do someone in" = to kill them, usually deliberately.

It is slang. It is not as clinical or formal as "murder" or "kill." It carries a slightly gritty, storytelling quality — the kind of language a detective novel uses.

Examples:

  • "The hitman was paid to do the witness in."
  • "Nobody knew who had done the old banker in."
  • "She was done in by her own business partner."
  • "They waited for the right moment and then did him in."

What to notice:

  • The past tense "did [someone] in" is very natural.
  • The passive "was done in" is also extremely common — it emphasises the victim, not the killer.
  • You will almost always hear this used about a person, not an animal or object.

Meaning 2 — To Exhaust Someone Completely

This is by far the most common meaning in everyday life. You will hear this constantly in British English, and regularly in other varieties too.

"To do someone in" = to leave them feeling completely and utterly drained — not just tired, but wiped out, with nothing left to give.

The exhaustion is total. This is not mild tiredness. It is the feeling after something physically or mentally brutal.

Examples:

  • "That 12-hour shift at the hospital totally did me in."
  • "Three back-to-back exams have really done her in."
  • "I'm absolutely done in after moving all those boxes." (Here "done in" works as a describing word meaning "completely exhausted.")
  • "The long climb up the mountain did us all in."
  • "Even just one hour of intense revision does him in."

What to notice:

  • "Done in" used on its own (without an object) acts like an adjective: "I'm done in" = "I'm completely wiped out."
  • The exhausting thing is usually a task, event, or experience — not a person.
  • This meaning is especially popular in British English, but it is well understood everywhere.

Meaning 3 — To Ruin or Destroy Someone (Career, Reputation, Chances)

This meaning is about downfall, not physical harm. It describes something that ends a person's career, destroys their reputation, or permanently ruins their prospects.

"To do someone in" = to bring about their ruin or failure.

Examples:

  • "The corruption scandal did the politician in." (= It ended his career.)
  • "His terrible temper eventually did him in at that company." (= It caused his downfall there.)
  • "One careless tweet did her in with the sponsors." (= It ruined that relationship.)
  • "The bad harvest and poor planning together did in the business." (= Together they destroyed it.)

What to notice:

  • The cause of the ruin is often not a person but a situation, a flaw, a mistake, or an event.
  • This meaning is about permanent damage — once someone is "done in" in this sense, they don't easily recover.
  • You can use it about a business, project, or plan — not just a person.

Meaning 4 — To Injure a Part of Your Body

This meaning is especially common in British and Australian English, though speakers of other varieties will understand it too.

"To do [a body part] in" = to hurt or injure it, usually through strain, overuse, or accident.

Examples:

  • "I did my back in lifting those heavy boxes."
  • "She did her knee in during the football match."
  • "He did his shoulder in at the gym last week."
  • "Be careful with that ladder — you'll do your ankle in."

What to notice:

  • The body part always sits between "do" and "in": "did my back in," "did her knee in."
  • The injury is typically from overexertion, awkward movement, or accident — not from someone attacking you (that would be Meaning 1).
  • This meaning feels very natural and conversational in British speech.
Grammar — How to Use "Do In" Correctly

"Do in" is what linguists call a separable phrasal verb. This means the object (the person or thing affected) can go between "do" and "in," or it can go after "in."

Rule 1 — When the object is a pronoun (me, him, her, them, us, it):
The pronoun must go between "do" and "in." You cannot put it after "in."

✅ "It did him in." (correct)
❌ "It did in him." (sounds wrong and unnatural)

✅ "That run did me in." (correct)
❌ "That run did in me." (sounds wrong)

Rule 2 — When the object is a noun or noun phrase:
You have a choice. Both positions work.

✅ "The scandal did the minister in."
✅ "The scandal did in the minister."

Both are grammatically fine. The first (object in the middle) tends to feel slightly more natural in speech.

Rule 3 — Passive voice:
The passive form is very common with "do in," especially for Meanings 1 and 2.

The passive is formed with "be done in":

  • "He was done in by his rivals." (killed)
  • "She was completely done in after the race." (exhausted)
  • "The project was done in by poor management." (ruined)
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "do in" has four meanings, you need context to identify the right one. Here are your four quick clues:

Someone is dead, or there is talk of killing → Meaning 1 (kill)
"The body was found. Someone had done him in."

Someone is exhausted after effort or hardship → Meaning 2 (exhaust completely)
"I'm done in after that gym session."

Someone's career, reputation, or plans are ruined → Meaning 3 (ruin/destroy)
"One bad decision did her in professionally."

A specific body part is mentioned → Meaning 4 (injure a body part)
"I've done my wrist in."

The meanings are distinct enough that confusion is rare in real speech. Context almost always makes it crystal clear.

"Do in" conjugates exactly like the verb "do":

  • Present: "This kind of work does me in."
  • Past simple: "That long hike did me in."
  • Present perfect: "The scandal has done him in."
  • Past perfect: "The injury had done her in long before the final."
  • Future: "This exam will do me in."
  • Continuous (less common but possible): "The heat is slowly doing us in."

"Do in" is solidly informal. Here is a simple breakdown:

Use it freely in:
Everyday conversation, text messages, casual emails to friends, fiction writing, film and TV dialogue, journalism (especially in informal or headline style).

Avoid it in:
Formal essays, academic writing, professional reports, official documents, business correspondence.

If you need a more formal equivalent, here are substitutes for each meaning:

  • Meaning 1 (kill): murder, kill, assassinate, eliminate
  • Meaning 2 (exhaust): exhaust, fatigue, drain, wear out
  • Meaning 3 (ruin): ruin, destroy, bring down, cause the downfall of
  • Meaning 4 (injure a body part): injure, strain, damage
A Brief Note on Why "In" Is There

This is a natural question. Why "in"? In many phrasal verbs, "in" carries a sense of finality or completion — bringing something all the way through to its end. Think of "hand in," "turn in," "fill in," "cash in" — the "in" often signals that something is being brought to a concluded state. In "do in," the "in" amplifies "do" to mean doing something all the way through, to a complete, often irreversible end. This is why all four meanings share that sense of something being finished off.

Knowing these nearby expressions helps you understand "do in" more fully and shows you how it fits into the broader family of English idioms:

"Done for" — completely ruined, with no hope left.
"After losing all his savings, he was done for."
(Similar to Meaning 3, but even more final and hopeless.)

"Finish off" — to kill or completely use up something; also to complete something.
"The frost finished off the remaining crops."
(Overlaps with Meaning 1.)

"Knock out" — to exhaust completely (informal).
"That run knocked me out."
(Overlaps with Meaning 2.)

"Worn out" — exhausted, depleted.
"I'm completely worn out."
(Synonym of the Meaning 2 result — but "worn out" describes a state, while "do in" describes the action that caused it.)

"Do away with" — to get rid of something or someone; can mean to kill, but is slightly more formal than "do in."
"He threatened to do away with his competitor."

"Bust up" — to injure (body), or to break a relationship (informal, common in British/Australian English).
"I've busted up my hip."
(Overlaps loosely with Meaning 4.)

"Do in" is a separable, informal phrasal verb with four meanings:

1. To kill — deliberate, used in crime and thriller contexts. "They did him in."

2. To exhaust completely — the most everyday use; total physical or mental depletion. "That shift did me in."

3. To ruin or destroy — bringing an end to someone's career, reputation, or plans. "His arrogance did him in."

4. To injure a body part — common in British and Australian English; the body part goes between "do" and "in." "I did my back in."

It is always informal. The object goes between "do" and "in" when the object is a pronoun. Context — especially what comes around the phrase — will always tell you which of the four meanings is at play.
